assessment_summary: The proof incorrectly claims that any infinite extension of $\hat\sigma = \sigma[..i]$ must also falsify the implication. Because the consequent is an eventual property ($\mathsf{F}(P1C \vee P2C)$), an extension can always satisfy it by making $P1C$ or $P2C$ true at some future index $>i$. Thus, the property is not a safety property, and the attempt to prove it is a safety property fails at step 0016.
counterexample: Let $\sigma = \{P1E, P2E\} \emptyset^\omega$. At $i=0$, $\sigma, 0 \not\Vdash (P1E \wedge P2E) \rightarrow \mathsf{F}(P1C \vee P2C)$. Then $\hat\sigma = \sigma[..0] = \{P1E, P2E\}$. The claim in 0016 states that for ANY word $\sigma^\prime$ with prefix $\hat\sigma$, $\sigma^\prime, i \not\Vdash (P1E \wedge P2E) \rightarrow \mathsf{F}(P1C \vee P2C)$. Consider $\sigma^\prime = \{P1E, P2E\} \{P1C\} \emptyset^\omega$. It has $\hat\sigma$ as a prefix, but $\sigma^\prime, 0 \Vdash (P1E \wedge P2E) \rightarrow \mathsf{F}(P1C \vee P2C)$ because $\sigma^\prime, 1 \Vdash P1C$, making $\mathsf{F}(P1C \vee P2C)$ true at $i=0$.
